questions.q: What are registers?
choices: Small pieces of physical memory located inside the CPU
Sections of RAM reserved for the operating system
Variables declared in a high-level language
Lookup tables the CPU uses to convert hex to binary
questions.explain: Registers are tiny storage locations built into the CPU itself. In assembly they replace the named variables (the 'boxes') of a high-level language.

questions.q: On an x86-64 system, how many bytes does each general-purpose register (such as RAX) hold?
questions.explain: Each general-purpose register on x86-64 is 8 bytes, which is 64 bits.

questions.q: The CPU prefers to do arithmetic directly on values in main memory rather than on values in registers.
questions.explain: The CPU can use memory, but it prefers to do arithmetic on values held in its registers.

questions.q: Compared with the number of variables a high-level program can declare, the CPU has only a small, fixed set of registers.
questions.explain: There are only a limited number of registers, so you have to choose carefully which values live in them.

questions.q: In the lesson's example of adding 3 and 4, which two registers stand in for the two 'boxes' that hold the values?
choices: RAX and RBX
RSI and RDI
RCX and RDX
RSP and RBP
questions.explain: 3 is placed in RAX and 4 in RBX, and then the two are added together.

questions.q: Besides the registers built on the letters A, B, C and D, two registers have names that come from the words 'destination' and 'source'. Which pair is it?
choices: RDI (destination) and RSI (source)
RDX (destination) and RSX (source)
RBP (destination) and RSP (source)
R8 (destination) and R9 (source)
questions.explain: RDI is the destination index register and RSI is the source index register.

questions.q: In a typical high-level language such as C, which set of sizes is most likely for int, long and char?
choices: int = 4 bytes, long = 8 bytes, char = 1 byte
int = 8 bytes, long = 4 bytes, char = 2 bytes
int = 2 bytes, long = 4 bytes, char = 4 bytes
int = 1 byte, long = 2 bytes, char = 8 bytes
questions.explain: An int is usually 4 bytes, a long is often 8 bytes on 64-bit systems, and a char is 1 byte. A 64-bit register is the same size as an 8-byte long.

questions.q: What form of instructions does the CPU actually execute?
choices: Binary machine code
Assembly mnemonics such as mov and add
Hexadecimal text
High-level source code
questions.explain: The CPU executes binary machine code. Hex is only a shorter way for people to write those bits, and assembly is a readable notation that has to be translated into them.

questions.q: Hexadecimal machine code is a separate instruction format that the CPU can run instead of binary.
questions.explain: Hex is just a more readable way to write the same binary bits. The instruction is identical whether you show it in hex or in binary.

questions.q: The instruction mov rax, 3 is encoded as the hex bytes 48 C7 C0 03 00 00 00. Each memory address holds one byte. How many bytes of memory does this instruction take up?
questions.explain: There are seven hex byte pairs (48, C7, C0, 03, 00, 00, 00), so the instruction fills seven consecutive one-byte memory addresses.

questions.q: Why is the machine code for add rax, rbx shorter than the machine code for mov rax, 3?
choices: add rax, rbx has no constant value (immediate) encoded inside the instruction
Addition is a simpler operation, so the CPU always uses fewer bits for it
RBX is a smaller register than RAX
add instructions are stored in hex while mov instructions are stored in binary
questions.explain: mov rax, 3 has to carry the value 3 inside the instruction bytes. add rax, rbx only names two registers, so its encoding is much shorter (3 bytes compared with 7).

questions.q: How does the CPU work out what a machine-code instruction means?
choices: Decoders check each bit of the instruction (0 or 1), and the result drives a matching set of control lines
It translates the instruction back into assembly text and reads the mnemonic
It looks up the instruction in a dictionary stored in RAM
It converts the bytes to decimal and compares them against a table
questions.explain: Instructions go through hardware decoders that check the bit pattern. The decoded pattern drives the control lines that make the CPU carry out the operation.

questions.q: mov rax, 3 and mov rbx, 4 assemble to identical machine code, because both are mov instructions.
questions.explain: Both are moves, but their encodings differ because the destination register and the constant value are encoded in the instruction bits.

questions.q: Which statement best describes assembly language?
choices: A human-readable notation that maps closely onto individual machine-code instructions
A high-level language that is compiled into C
The hexadecimal representation of binary
A language the CPU runs directly without any translation
questions.explain: Assembly uses short mnemonics such as mov and add to stand for machine instructions. It is much easier to read than binary but stays very close to it.

questions.q: Assembly language grew out of the notes early programmers wrote to describe binary instructions in more readable terms.
questions.explain: Shorthand notes such as 'move into A the value 3' were shortened to forms like 'mov a, 3', and that became assembly language.

questions.q: Where does assembly sit compared with machine code and high-level languages?
choices: In between: more readable than machine code, but much closer to the hardware than high-level languages
Below machine code: it is what the CPU's decoders produce
Above high-level languages: it is the most English-like form
It is the same as machine code, just shown in hex
questions.explain: Machine code is the bits the CPU runs. Assembly brings those bits back as close to English as is practical, and high-level languages go much further toward English.

questions.q:
After these instructions run, which statements are true?

mov rax, 3
mov rbx, 4
add rax, rbx
choices: RAX holds 7
RBX holds 4
RBX holds 7
RAX holds 3
questions.explain: add rax, rbx adds the value in RBX into RAX, so RAX becomes 3 + 4 = 7. RBX is only read, so it still holds 4.

questions.q: Write the assembly instruction, in the form used in the lesson, that puts the value 3 into register RAX.
questions.explain: mov rax, 3 means 'move into RAX the value 3'. The destination comes first and the source second.

questions.q: Write the assembly instruction, in the form used in the lesson, that adds the value in RBX into RAX and keeps the result in RAX.
questions.explain: add rax, rbx means 'add into RAX the value of RBX'. The result goes in the first operand, RAX.

questions.q: What does an assembler, such as FASM (the flat assembler) or the GNU assembler, do?
choices: Converts assembly instructions into binary machine code
Runs high-level programs line by line
Translates binary machine code into English sentences
Chooses which registers a C compiler should use
questions.explain: An assembler is a program that turns your assembly instructions into the binary the CPU executes.

questions.q: Different assemblers, such as FASM and the GNU assembler, can use different directives and options, even though both turn instructions into binary.
questions.explain: They are just two programs that do the same basic job. Each has its own metadata/directive conventions and options.

questions.q: How many bits does a single hexadecimal digit represent?
questions.explain: One hex digit covers exactly one 4-bit group (0000 to 1111).

questions.q: Why does hexadecimal fit binary better than decimal does?
choices: 4 bits have 16 possible combinations, and hex has exactly 16 single digits (0-9, A-F), so every combination gets its own digit; decimal's 10 digits leave 6 combinations unused
Hex uses fewer bits than binary to store the same value in memory
Decimal cannot represent numbers greater than 9
The CPU executes hex digits faster than decimal digits
questions.explain: Decimal stops at 9 even though 4 bits can go up to 15. Hex adds the six digits A-F (10-15), so every 4-bit pattern is a single digit.

questions.q: What decimal value does the hex digit F represent?
questions.explain: A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. F is 1111, the largest 4-bit value.

questions.q: Convert hex 5B to 8-bit binary.
questions.explain: 5 = 0101 and B = 1011. Put them together to get 0101 1011.

questions.q: Convert binary 0100 1000 to hex. (This is the first byte of the encoding of mov rax, 3.)
questions.explain: 0100 = 4 and 1000 = 8, so the byte is 48 in hex.

questions.q: Convert hex C7 to 8-bit binary.
Which 4-bit binary pattern is the hex digit D?
To turn a long binary value into hex, split it into 4-bit groups and replace each group with one hex digit.
questions.explain: Each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so the conversion works one group at a time in either direction, with no arithmetic on the whole number.
